<reason>Both sides executed at a high level with clean A1/A2 compliance and sharp framing. A wins on the arithmetic of the clash: B's rarity/rationing pillar was dismantled (rare means a trivial budget line; the prevented intensive care costs far more; B never answered the savings comparison after A4.1-A4.2), and A took the slope clash decisively with "have that debate then" plus the closing point that the motion's own words already restrict funding to preventing severe mitochondrial disease. A's equity framing (licensed for the rich, ventilator for the poor) stayed sticky even after B's coherent license-to-learn reply. B's best material — the experimental-drug licensing analogy, the mito-nuclear "untested chassis" point, and the late non-identity/preference argument — was genuinely strong and never fully rebutted on the preference question, but B left the cost pillar collapsed and closed more on recap of that ground than on new resolution. Minor execution costs on both sides (clipped turns) roughly cancel.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive exchange was A's Rebuttal 1 catching "private access under license" and forcing B to defend funding-not-safety, followed by B's strong B2.1 drug-licensing recovery ("we license experimental drugs; we do not put them on the formulary"). B won that individual exchange, but A's parallel dismantling of the rarity/cost argument — showing prevention is cheaper than the ventilator and that B's own sickle-cell comparator costs millions — was the blow B never answered, and it decided the debate.</best_rebuttal>
